# Solving X2-Y2-Z4

## What the known tasks pin down

**Y components (which bit)**
- **Y2 = bit 4.** In X6-Y2-Z3, every yellow input has bit 4 equal to 1 in both stimuli.
- **Y4 = bit 1.** In X6-Y4-Z3, the yellow inputs are exactly those with bit 1 equal to 1 in both stimuli.
- **Y3 = bit 3.** In X6-Y3-Z2, the green inputs are exactly those with bit 3 equal to 1 in both stimuli.
- **Y1 = bit 2.** Only bit 2 fits X5-Y1-Z2.

**X components (the rule)**
- **X6 = "both are 1".**
- **X5 = "exactly one is 1".** This fits both X5-Y1-Z2 and X5-Y3-Z4.

**Z components (which button for true and false)**

| Z | Rule true | Rule false |
|---|---|---|
| Z3 | yellow | green |
| Z2 | green | blue |
| Z4 | blue | red |

## The open question: X2 and Z1

In X2-Y2-Z1, the output is red exactly when bit 4 is 0 in both stimuli. Two assignments fit every example:

- **(a)** X2 = "at least one is 1", and Z1 gives green when true, red when false.
- **(b)** X2 = "neither is 1", and Z1 gives red when true, green when false.

No other combination fits. These two readings give opposite answers for every item in the new task.

## Choosing between them

Look at the "true" buttons across the Z components:
- Under (b), the true buttons are Z1 red, Z2 green, Z3 yellow and Z4 blue. Each Z has a different true button, covering all four.
- Under (a), Z1 and Z2 would both give green when true.

That one-to-one pattern makes (b) more plausible. I'll go with it, but it is a judgment call, not something the examples prove.

## Predictions

Under (b), X2-Y2-Z4 gives **blue** when bit 4 is 0 in both stimuli, and **red** otherwise.

| # | Input | Bit 4 pair | Button |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1001 0110 | 1, 0 | red |
| 2 | 1001 0100 | 1, 0 | red |
| 3 | 0010 1001 | 0, 1 | red |
| 4 | 0111 1000 | 1, 0 | red |
| 5 | 1100 0101 | 0, 1 | red |
| 6 | 0000 0001 | 0, 1 | red |
| 7 | 1101 1110 | 1, 0 | red |
| 8 | 1000 0110 | 0, 0 | blue |
| 9 | 0100 1011 | 0, 1 | red |
| 10 | 0101 1101 | 1, 1 | red |
| 11 | 0010 1010 | 0, 0 | blue |
| 12 | 1101 0111 | 1, 1 | red |
| 13 | 1011 0110 | 1, 0 | red |
| 14 | 1100 1000 | 0, 0 | blue |
| 15 | 1100 0000 | 0, 0 | blue |
| 16 | 1000 1100 | 0, 0 | blue |

The answers are not determined, because reading (a) would flip every one. My confidence of about 0.6 reflects how far I trust the pattern argument.

# Learn tasks from examples

Each task maps an input to one of four buttons: green, blue, red, or yellow. An input is a pair of stimuli; each stimulus has 4 binary features, written as 4 bits (bit positions 1-4, left to right). The line `1011 0110 -> red` means: stimulus 1 is 1011, stimulus 2 is 0110, and the correct button is red.

Every task is built from three components. A **Y component** picks one of the 4 features (bit positions 1-4); the task looks at that feature in both stimuli. An **X component** is a rule on those two bits, one of: both are 1; at least one is 1; exactly one is 1; neither is 1; not both are 1; both are the same. A **Z component** gives one button when the rule is true and a different button when it is false. A task's label lists its components, for example X2-Y1-Z3. Each kind has several versions (X1, X2, and so on); different versions of a kind are different from each other, and the same label always means the same component. You are not told which version does what.
